title: Theorem A
head: environment
name: \(\Gamma\)-expansion and entropic selection

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\). Since \(\gamma\) has marginals \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\), strong duality gives \(\int_\Omega\overline\varphi_1\oplus\overline\varphi_2\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma=\mathsf{OT}(\mu_1,\mu_2)\), hence \(\int_\Omega c\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma=\mathsf{OT}(\mu_1,\mu_2)+\int_\Omega E\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma\). Moreover, since \(E\) is bounded, the measures \(\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\) and \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) are equivalent, with bounded log-density \(\log\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}}{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)}=-\frac{E}{\varepsilon}-\log Z_\varepsilon\), so that
\[
\varepsilon\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)
=
\varepsilon\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon})
-\int_\Omega E\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma
-\varepsilon\log Z_\varepsilon,
\]
both sides being possibly infinite. Summing the two identities gives \eqref{eq: EOT-Gibbs identity}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(E\geq0\) and \(E=0\) on \(\Sigma\), we have
\(\nabla E=0\) on \(\Sigma\), and \(\operatorname{Hess} E(z)\) is positive
semidefinite there. Differentiating \(\nabla E=0\) along
\(\Sigma\) gives \(T_z\Sigma\subseteq\ker\operatorname{Hess} E(z)\).
The separated form of the potentials implies
\(D^2_{x_1x_2}E=D^2_{x_1x_2}c\) near \(\Sigma\): this identity
also follows directly by taking mixed differences, without initially
assuming differentiability of the potentials.
Thus the mixed block of \(\operatorname{Hess} E(z)\) has rank \(d\), so
\(\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{Hess} E(z)\geq d\). The preceding kernel
inclusion and \(\dim T_z\Sigma=d\) give the reverse inequality.
Consequently, \(\ker\operatorname{Hess} E(z)=T_z\Sigma\).

The differential of \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}^\Sigma_{M_1}\) at \(z\) is the restriction of \((u,v)\mapsto u\) to \(T_z\Sigma\), whose kernel consists of the vectors \((0,v)\in T_z\Sigma=\ker\operatorname{Hess} E(z)\). For such a vector, the first component of \(\operatorname{Hess} E(z)[(0,v)]=0\) reads \(D^2_{x_1x_2}c(z)v=0\), whence \(v=0\). Thus \(D\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}^\Sigma_{M_1}(z)\) is injective, hence an isomorphism since \(\dim T_z\Sigma=d=\dim M_1\), and the inverse function theorem shows that \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}^\Sigma_{M_1}\) is a local \(C^{1,1}\) diffeomorphism. The same argument applies to \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}^\Sigma_{M_2}\).
Finally, positive semidefiniteness and the kernel identity \(\ker\operatorname{Hess} E(z)=T_z\Sigma\) make the restriction \(H_{z}E\) of \(\operatorname{Hess} E(z)\) to \(N_z\Sigma=(T_z\Sigma)^\perp\) positive definite. Continuity of the Hessian and the normal
spaces, together with compactness of \(\Sigma\), gives
\eqref{eq: normal-ellipticity}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{prop: twist-geometry}, the projection \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}^\Sigma_{M_1}\) is a local \(C^{1,1}\) diffeomorphism, so that, locally, \(\Sigma\) is the graph of a \(C^{1,1}\) map \(x_1\mapsto x_2\). Identifying the tangent spaces of the flat tori with \(\mathbb{R}^d\), this means that, for every \(z\in\Sigma\), \(T_z\Sigma=\{(u,B(z)u):u\in\mathbb{R}^d\}\) for some matrix \(B(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\), where \(z\mapsto B(z)\) is locally Lipschitz, hence Lipschitz on \(\Sigma\) by compactness. Hence \(N_z\Sigma=\{(-B(z)^\top w,w):w\in\mathbb{R}^d\}\), that is, the columns of
\[
N(z)\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\begin{pmatrix}
-B(z)^\top\\
I_d
\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d\times k}
\]
form a basis of \(N_z\Sigma\). Since their Gram matrix \(N(z)^\top N(z)=I_d+B(z)B(z)^\top\) is symmetric positive definite, we obtain an orthonormal basis of \(N_z\Sigma\) by setting
\[
n(z)
\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}
N(z)\bigl(I_d+B(z)B(z)^\top\bigr)^{-1/2},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
n(z)^\top n(z)=I_k .
\]
The map \(n\) is Lipschitz, as \(B\) is.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix \(z\in\Sigma\) at which \(n\) is differentiable along \(\Sigma\). Since \(\Phi(z,s)=z+n(z)s\) is affine in \(s\), the map \(\Phi\) is differentiable at \((z,s)\) for every \(s\in\mathbb{B}_{r_0}\), and, for \(X\in T_z\Sigma\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}^k\),
\[
D\Phi(z,s)[X,t]
=
X+\sum_{p=1}^{k}s_pDn_p(z)[X]+n(z)t
=
\bigl(X+G(z,s)X\bigr)+Q(z,s)X+n(z)t,
\]
where \(Q(z,s)X\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_{N_z\Sigma}\bigl(\sum_{p=1}^{k}s_pDn_p(z)[X]\bigr)\in N_z\Sigma\). Hence, decomposing the target space as \(\mathbb{R}^{2d}=T_z\Sigma\oplus N_z\Sigma\), the operator \(D\Phi(z,s):T_z\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}^k\to T_z\Sigma\oplus N_z\Sigma\) has the block lower triangular form
\[
D\Phi(z,s)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{Id}_{T_z\Sigma}+G(z,s) & 0_{\mathbb{R}^k\to T_z\Sigma}\\
Q(z,s) & n(z)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Let \((e_1,\ldots,e_d)\) be an orthonormal basis of \(T_z\Sigma\). By \Cref{lemma: normal-frame}, the vectors \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\), \(n_1(z),\ldots,n_k(z)\) form an orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb{R}^{2d}\), in which the block \(n(z)\) has matrix \(I_k\). Computing \(\mathcal J_\Phi(z,s)\) in this basis and in the orthonormal basis of \(T_z\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}^k\) formed by \((e_1,\ldots,e_d)\) and the canonical basis of \(\mathbb{R}^k\), we obtain \(\mathcal J_\Phi(z,s)=\bigl|\det\bigl(\operatorname{Id}_{T_z\Sigma}+G(z,s)\bigr)\bigr|\). Finally, denoting by \(\operatorname{Lip}(n)\) the Lipschitz constant of \(n\), we have \(\|G_p(z)\|\leq\|Dn_p(z)\|\leq\operatorname{Lip}(n)\) for every \(p\), whence \(\|G(z,s)\|\leq\sum_{p=1}^{k}|s_p|\,\|G_p(z)\|\leq\sqrt k\operatorname{Lip}(n)|s|\).

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(r_0>0\) be as in \Cref{subsec:structure}, and let
\(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}\in\Sigma_{r_0}\). Then \(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}=\Phi(z,s)\) with \(z=\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_\Sigma(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})\) and a unique \(s\in\mathbb{B}_{r_0}\), and \(|s|=\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\Sigma)\) by \eqref{eq: normal-distance}. Since \(z\) is a minimum point of \(E\geq0\), one has \(E(z)=0\) and \(\nabla E(z)=0\), so that a Taylor expansion of \(E\) gives
\[
E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
=
\frac{1}{2}H_{z}E(s,s)
+
\mathcal R(z,s),
\qquad
\mathcal R(z,s)=O\bigl(|s|^3\bigr)
\quad\text{as }s\to0,
\]
uniformly with respect to \(z\in\Sigma\), since \(E\) belongs to \(C^{2,1}(\Omega)\).
By \eqref{eq: normal-ellipticity}, \(\lambda |s|^2 \leq H_{z}E(s,s) \leq \Lambda |s|^2\).
Taking \(r<r_0\) small enough, we have \(|\mathcal R(z,s)|\leq\frac{\lambda}{4}|s|^2\) whenever \(z\in\Sigma\) and \(|s|\leq r\).
Consequently,
\[
\frac{\lambda}{4}\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\Sigma)^2
\leq
E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
\leq
\frac{3\Lambda}{4}\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\Sigma)^2,
\]
and the conclusion follows by setting \(
\underline{C}\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\frac{\lambda}{4}\) and \(
\overline{C}\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\frac{3\Lambda}{4}\).

label: thm: convergence-Gibbs-measure
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: convergence-Gibbs-measure}
Under \ref{H1}--\ref{H4}, as \(\varepsilon\to0\), the Gibbs measure \(\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\) converges weakly to a probability measure \(\mathbb{P}_0\), given by
\[
\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_0(z)
=
\frac{1}{Z_0}
\left(\det H_{z}E\right)^{-1/2}
\rho(z)
\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}(z),
\qquad
Z_0
\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}
\int_\Sigma
\left(\det H_{z}E\right)^{-1/2}
\rho(z)
\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}(z).
\]
Moreover, \(Z_\varepsilon=(2\pi\varepsilon)^{k/2}(Z_0+o(1))\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq: normal-recovery-density}, and since \(\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\) has density \(Z_\varepsilon^{-1}e^{-E/\varepsilon}\rho\) with respect to \(\operatorname{vol}_\Omega\), where \(\rho\) is the density of \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\), we have, for \(\mathcal H^d\)-a.e.\ \(z\in\Sigma\) and every \(s\in\mathbb{B}_R\),
\begin{align*}
 \log\left(
 \frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}}
      {\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}}(\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s))\right)
 &=\log\overline\rho(z)
   +\log\left(\frac{Z_\varepsilon}
   {\varepsilon^{k/2}Z_R(z)}\right)
   -\log\rho(\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s))
\\
 &\qquad+\frac{E(\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s))-\frac12H_{z}E(\sqrt\varepsilon s,\sqrt\varepsilon s)}
 {\varepsilon}
 -\log\mathcal J_\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s).
\end{align*}
As in the proof of \Cref{lemma: quadratic-detachment}, a Taylor expansion of \(E\) gives
\[
E(\Phi(z,\eta))=\frac12H_{z}E(\eta,\eta)+\mathcal R(z,\eta),
\qquad
|\mathcal R(z,\eta)|\leq C|\eta|^3.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon})=\int_\Omega\log\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}}{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\), we may compute this integral in tubular coordinates by \eqref{eq: recovery sequence with wrong marginals 1}, that is, integrate the above identity against \(K_R(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma(z)\). We obtain
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon} \right)
 &=\int_\Sigma\log\overline\rho(z)\overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z)
 +\int_\Sigma\log\left(\frac{Z_\varepsilon}
 {\varepsilon^{k/2}Z_R(z)}\right)
 \overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z)
 \\
 &\qquad-\int_\Sigma\int_{\mathbb{B}_R}
 \Bigl(\log\rho(\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s))
       -\frac{\mathcal R(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)}{\varepsilon}
 \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad
       +\log\mathcal J_\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)\Bigr)
 K_R(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\,\overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z).
\end{align*}
These integrals are finite: since \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\) and the density of \(\mathbb P_0\) with respect to \(\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\) is bounded from above and below by positive constants, we have
\(\int_\Sigma|\log\overline\rho|\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma<\infty\).
Since \(|\mathcal R(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)|\leq C\varepsilon^{3/2}|s|^3\), since \(\log\rho\) is Lipschitz (\(\rho\) being Lipschitz and bounded below by a positive constant), and since \(|\log\mathcal J_\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)|\leq C\sqrt\varepsilon|s|\) by \eqref{eq: tube-jacobian-rescaled}, the double integral in the last line differs from \(\int_\Sigma\log\rho\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma\) by at most
\[
C\sqrt\varepsilon\int_\Sigma\int_{\mathbb{B}_R}\bigl(|s|+|s|^3\bigr)K_R(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\,\overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z)\leq C\sqrt\varepsilon\longrightarrow0,
\]
by \eqref{eq: gaussian-moments}.
Moreover, by \Cref{thm: convergence-Gibbs-measure},
\(Z_\varepsilon=(2\pi\varepsilon)^{k/2}(Z_0+o(1))\), so that, uniformly in \(z\),
\[
 \log\left(\frac{Z_\varepsilon}
 {\varepsilon^{k/2}Z_R(z)}\right)
 =\log\frac{(2\pi)^{k/2}Z_0}{Z_R(z)}+o(1)
 =\log\left(Z_0\sqrt{\det H_{z}E}\right)
  +\log\frac{Z_\infty(z)}{Z_R(z)}+o(1).
\]
Combining these identities yields
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon} \right)
 &\longrightarrow
 \int_\Sigma\log\frac{\overline\rho(z)}{\rho(z)}\overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z)
 +\int_\Sigma\log\left(Z_0\sqrt{\det H_{z}E}\right)
 \overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z)
 \\
 &\qquad+\int_\Sigma\log\frac{Z_\infty(z)}{Z_R(z)}
 \overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z)
 \\
 &=\operatorname{Ent}\left(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0\right)+b_R(\overline\gamma).
\end{align*}
Finally, the Gaussian tail estimate
\[
 0\leq Z_\infty(z)-Z_R(z)
 \leq\int_{|s|\geq R}\exp\left(-\frac{\lambda}{2}|s|^2\right)\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s
 \longrightarrow0\qquad(R\to\infty)
\]
is uniform in \(z\). Together with \(Z_R(z)\geq c>0\), this shows
that \(b_R\geq0\) tends to zero uniformly over probability measures
on \(\Sigma\), and proves the claim.

label: def: shadow
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def: shadow} 
Let \(\mu_i, \widetilde{\mu}_i \in \mathcal{P}(M_i)\) with \(\widetilde\mu_i\ll\operatorname{vol}_{M_i}\), and let \(T_i\) denote the optimal transport map from \(\widetilde \mu_i\) to \(\mu_i\) for the quadratic cost, \(i=1,2\). Then, for a given \(\widetilde{\gamma} \in \Pi(\widetilde{\mu}_1,\widetilde\mu_2)\), its \emph{shadow} \(\gamma \in \Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) is defined by
\[
\gamma \stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} \big(T_1,T_2\big)_\# \widetilde{\gamma}.
\]
head: environment
name: Shadow

title: Proof
body_md:
In this proof, we write \(\gamma=\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\), \(\widetilde\gamma=\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) and \(\widetilde\mu_i=\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\). Recall that \(\mathbb P_\varepsilon=f_\varepsilon\,\mu^\otimes\), where \(f_\varepsilon\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} Z_\varepsilon^{-1}e^{-E/\varepsilon}\) (\Cref{prop: EOT-Gibbs}).
By \Cref{lemma: convergence entropy}, \(\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon})<\infty\), hence \(\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\mu^\otimes)\le\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon})-\log Z_\varepsilon<\infty\) since \(E\geq0\).
Hence the marginal entropies \(\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\mu_i\,|\,\mu_i)\) are finite by projection, and so are all the
quantities below. By a change of reference measure, \(\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon})=\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot\,|\,\mu^\otimes)-\int_\Omega\log f_\varepsilon\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\cdot)\) on probability measures. Together with \Cref{prop: bound entropy shadow}, this gives
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Ent}\left(\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\right)
 &=\operatorname{Ent}\left(\gamma\,|\,\mu^\otimes\right)
 -\int_\Omega\log f_\varepsilon\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma
 \\
 &\leq\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\widetilde\mu_1\otimes\widetilde\mu_2\right)
 -\int_\Omega\log f_\varepsilon\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma\\
 &=\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\right)
 +\int_\Omega\log f_\varepsilon\,
 \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\widetilde\gamma-\gamma)
 \\
 &\qquad+\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\widetilde\mu_1\otimes\widetilde\mu_2\right) -\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\mu^\otimes\right).
\end{align*}
Since \(\widetilde\mu_i\ll\mu_i\) (\Cref{subsec: normal-recovery}), there exist
Borel functions \(a_i:M_i\to[0,\infty)\) such that
\(\widetilde\mu_i=a_i\,\mu_i\), so that
\(\widetilde\mu_1\otimes\widetilde\mu_2=a_1(x_1)a_2(x_2)\,\mu^\otimes\).
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\widetilde\mu_1\otimes\widetilde\mu_2\right)-\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\mu^\otimes\right)
 &=-\int_\Omega\log\bigl(a_1(x_1)a_2(x_2)\bigr)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma(x_1,x_2)
 \\
 &=-\sum_{i=1}^2\int_{M_i}\log a_i\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\mu_i
 =-\sum_{i=1}^2\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\mu_i\,|\,\mu_i\right)\leq0,
\end{align*}
where the last inequality follows from the nonnegativity of the relative
entropy between probability measures. Finally, since \(\log f_\varepsilon=-E/\varepsilon-\log Z_\varepsilon\) and both plans have total mass one,
\[
 \operatorname{Ent}\left(\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon} \right)
\leq\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\right)
 -\int_\Omega\log f_\varepsilon\,
 \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\gamma-\widetilde\gamma)
=\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\right)
 +\frac1\varepsilon\int_\Omega E\,
 \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\gamma-\widetilde\gamma).
\]

label: thm: Wasserstein between the marginals
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Marginal estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(T_{\varepsilon,R}\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}(T_1,T_2)\), where \(T_i\) is the optimal transport map from \(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\) to \(\mu_i\). By definition of the shadow,
\(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}
 =(T_{\varepsilon,R})_\#\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\).
Set
\[
 \Delta_{\varepsilon,R}^2
 \stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}))^2
 \,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
 =\sum_{i=1}^2W_2^2(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R},\mu_i).
\]
The pushforward identity gives
\[
 \frac1\varepsilon\int_\Omega E\,
 \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}-\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})
 =\frac1\varepsilon\int_\Omega
 \bigl(E(T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}))-E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})\bigr)
 \,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}).
\]

We identify \(\Omega\) with \(\mathbb T^{2d}=\mathbb{R}^{2d}/\mathbb Z^{2d}\), denote by \([y]\in\Omega\) the class of \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}\), and by \(\widetilde E\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} E([\,\cdot\,])\) the \(\mathbb Z^{2d}\)-periodic lift of \(E\), which belongs to \(C^{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{2d})\) by \ref{H2}. We set
\[
 C_E\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\|D^2\widetilde E(y)\|<\infty,
\]
where \(\|\cdot\|\) denotes the operator norm.

We first estimate the gradient by the distance to \(\Sigma\). Let \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}\). Since \(\Sigma\) is compact, there exists \(\bar y\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}\) such that \([\bar y]\in\Sigma\) and \(|y-\bar y|=\operatorname{dist}([y],\Sigma)\). Since \(\nabla\widetilde E(\bar y)=0\), the fundamental theorem of calculus gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: gradient-distance}
 |\nabla\widetilde E(y)|
 =\left|\int_0^1 D^2\widetilde E\bigl(\bar y+t(y-\bar y)\bigr)(y-\bar y)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} t\right|
 \leq C_E\operatorname{dist}([y],\Sigma).
\end{equation}
Now, for each \(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}\in\Omega\), choose \(\widetilde\operatorname{\textbf{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}\) with \([\widetilde\operatorname{\textbf{x}}]=\operatorname{\textbf{x}}\), and a shortest displacement \(v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}\in\mathbb R^{2d}\) such that
\[
 [\widetilde\operatorname{\textbf{x}}+v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}]=T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}),
 \qquad |v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}|=\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})).
\]
By the fundamental theorem of calculus,
\[
 E(T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}))-E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
 =\widetilde E(\widetilde\operatorname{\textbf{x}}+v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}})-\widetilde E(\widetilde\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
 =\int_0^1\bigl\langle\nabla\widetilde E(\widetilde\operatorname{\textbf{x}}+\tau v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}),
                         v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}\bigr\rangle\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\tau.
\]
For every \(\tau\in[0,1]\), the triangle inequality gives \(\operatorname{dist}([\widetilde\operatorname{\textbf{x}}+\tau v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}],\Sigma)\leq\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\Sigma)+\tau|v_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}|\). Together with \eqref{eq: gradient-distance}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: energy-difference-gradient}
 |E(T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}))-E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})|
 \leq C_E \operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}))
              \operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\Sigma)
 +C_E \operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},T_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}))^2.
\end{equation}
Integrating \eqref{eq: energy-difference-gradient} with respect to \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) and applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac1\varepsilon\left|\int_\Omega E\,
 \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}-\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})\right|
 &\leq\frac{C_E\Delta_{\varepsilon,R}}{\varepsilon}
 \left(\int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\Sigma)^2
 \,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})\right)^{1/2}
 \\
 &\qquad+\frac{C_E\Delta_{\varepsilon,R}^2}{\varepsilon}.
\end{align*}
Recalling the definition \eqref{eq: recovery sequence with wrong marginals 1} of \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) and using \eqref{eq: normal-distance}, we have
\[
 \int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\Sigma)^2
 \,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
 =\varepsilon\int_\Sigma
 \int_{\mathbb{B}_R}|s|^2
 K_R(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\,\overline\gamma(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z)
 \leq M_2\,\varepsilon,
\]
by \eqref{eq: gaussian-moments}.
Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: shadow-energy-diagonal}
 \frac1\varepsilon\left|\int_\Omega E\,
 \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}-\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})\right|
 \leq C\left(\frac{\Delta_{\varepsilon,R}}{\sqrt\varepsilon}
            +\frac{\Delta_{\varepsilon,R}^2}{\varepsilon}\right).
\end{equation}
For fixed \(R\), \Cref{thm: Wasserstein between the marginals}
gives \(\Delta_{\varepsilon,R}=o_R(\sqrt\varepsilon)\), so that
both terms on the right-hand side tend to zero.

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Step 1. The \(\Gamma\)-\(\liminf\) inequality \eqref{eq: gamma-liminf}.} Let \(\gamma_\varepsilon\rightharpoonup\overline\gamma\). If \(\overline\gamma\notin\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\), then, since \(\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) is closed, \(\gamma_\varepsilon\notin\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) for \(\varepsilon\) small enough, so that \(\mathcal G_\varepsilon(\gamma_\varepsilon)=+\infty\). Otherwise, the joint lower semicontinuity of the relative entropy, together with the convergence \(\mathbb P_\varepsilon\rightharpoonup\mathbb P_0\) given by \Cref{thm: convergence-Gibbs-measure}, yields
\[
\liminf_{\varepsilon\to0}\mathcal G_\varepsilon(\gamma_\varepsilon)
\geq\liminf_{\varepsilon\to0} \operatorname{Ent}\left( \gamma_\varepsilon \,\middle\vert\, \mathbb{P}_\varepsilon \right) \geq \operatorname{Ent}\left( \overline \gamma \,\middle\vert\, \mathbb{P}_0 \right)=\mathcal G_0(\overline\gamma).
\]

\textbf{Step 2. The \(\Gamma\)-\(\limsup\) inequality \eqref{eq: gamma-limsup}.} Let \(\overline\gamma\in\mathcal P(\Omega)\) with \(\mathcal G_0(\overline\gamma)<\infty\) (otherwise there is nothing to prove). For \(R\geq1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(\sqrt\varepsilon R<r_0\), let \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) be the normal perturbation of \(\overline\gamma\) defined in \eqref{eq: recovery sequence with wrong marginals 1}, and \(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\in\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) its shadow. We first fix \(R\). By \Cref{lemma: convergence entropy}, \Cref{prop: control of the shadow entropy} and \Cref{prop: shadow-energy},
\[
 \limsup_{\varepsilon\to0}\mathcal G_\varepsilon(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})
 =\limsup_{\varepsilon\to0}\operatorname{Ent}\left(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\right)
 \leq\mathcal G_0(\overline\gamma)+b_R(\overline\gamma),
\]
while \Cref{prop: bound entropy shadow} and \eqref{eq: normal-perturbation-W2} give
\[
W_2(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R},\overline\gamma)
\leq W_2(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R},\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})+W_2(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R},\overline\gamma)
\leq(\sqrt2+1)\sqrt\varepsilon R
\longrightarrow0
\qquad(\varepsilon\to0),
\]
so that \(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\rightharpoonup\overline\gamma\), since \(W_2\) metrizes the weak convergence on the compact set \(\Omega\). Hence \((\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})_{\varepsilon}\) is a recovery sequence for \(\overline\gamma\) up to the error \(b_R(\overline\gamma)\), which tends to \(0\) as \(R\to\infty\) by \Cref{lemma: convergence entropy}. As is standard in \(\Gamma\)-convergence, this suffices to obtain a recovery sequence by a diagonal argument (see, e.g., \cite{dalmaso1993introduction}), which we recall for completeness. Choose \(R_j\uparrow\infty\) and, inductively, \(\varepsilon_j\downarrow0\) such that, for every \(0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_j\), we have \(\sqrt\varepsilon R_j<r_0\),
\(W_2(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R_j},\overline\gamma)\leq1/j\), and
\(\mathcal G_\varepsilon(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R_j})\leq\mathcal G_0(\overline\gamma)+b_{R_j}(\overline\gamma)+1/j\).
Then \(\gamma_\varepsilon\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\gamma_{\varepsilon,R_j}\) for \(\varepsilon_{j+1}<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_j\) defines a recovery sequence for \(\overline\gamma\).

\textbf{Step 3. Conclusion.}
By \eqref{eq: G-vs-F}, \eqref{eq: gamma-expansion} follows from
the \(\Gamma\)-convergence of \(\mathcal G_\varepsilon\) to \(\mathcal G_0\) established in Steps~1 and~2, since adding to \(\mathcal G_\varepsilon\) constants converging as \(\varepsilon\to0\) does not affect \(\Gamma\)-convergence.
The infimum of \(\mathcal F^{(1)}\) is finite. Indeed, since relative entropies are nonnegative, \(\mathcal F^{(1)}\geq-\log Z_0-\frac k2\log(2\pi)\), and it suffices to show that every optimal transport plan \(\overline\gamma\) satisfies \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\). By \eqref{eq: optimality-support}, such a plan satisfies \(\overline\gamma(\Omega\setminus\Sigma)=0\). For every Borel set \(A\subseteq\Sigma\), since \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_{M_1}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz, we have
\[
\overline\gamma(A)
\leq\mu_1\bigl(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_{M_1}(A)\bigr)
\leq\beta\,\mathcal H^d\bigl(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_{M_1}(A)\bigr)
\leq\beta\,\mathcal H^d(A),
\]
so that \(\overline\gamma\leq\beta\,\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\). Since the density of \(\mathbb P_0\) with respect to \(\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\) is bounded from below by a positive constant, by \ref{H4} and the continuity of \(\operatorname{Hess}^\perp E\) on the compact set \(\Sigma\), the density of \(\overline\gamma\) with respect to \(\mathbb P_0\) is bounded, hence \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\).
Compactness and convergence of minima under \(\Gamma\)-convergence
then give \eqref{eq: energy-expansion}.

For (iii), note that, by \Cref{prop: EOT-Gibbs}, \(\mathcal F_\varepsilon\) and \(\mathcal G_\varepsilon\) have the same minimizers, and so do \(\mathcal F^{(1)}\) and \(\mathcal G_0\). Since \(\mathcal P(\Omega)\) is weakly compact and the functionals \(\mathcal G_\varepsilon\), \(\mathcal G_0\) are lower semicontinuous, strictly convex on their domains and not identically \(+\infty\), they admit unique minimizers \(\gamma_\varepsilon\) and \(\gamma_0\). By the fundamental theorem of \(\Gamma\)-convergence (see, e.g., \cite{dalmaso1993introduction}), every cluster point of \((\gamma_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}\) as \(\varepsilon\to0\) minimizes \(\mathcal G_0\), hence \(\gamma_\varepsilon\rightharpoonup\gamma_0\). Finally, since \(\mathcal G_0(\gamma_0)<\infty\), we have \(\gamma_0\ll\mathbb P_0\), so that \(\operatorname{spt}(\gamma_0)\subseteq\Sigma\) and \(\gamma_0\) is an optimal transport plan by \eqref{eq: optimality-support}, hence the unique minimizer of \(\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot\,|\,\mathbb P_0)\) among all optimal transport plans.

title: Proof
body_md:
Throughout the proof, we still denote by \(\mu\) the density of \(\mu\). For \(t\in[0,1]\), let
\[
\mu_{t,\varepsilon}
\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\mu*(x\mapsto t\sqrt\varepsilon x)_\#
\left[\frac{1}{c_R}e^{-x^2/2}
\mathbf1_{\{|x|\le R\}}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} x\right],
\]
where convolution and push-forward are understood as operations on
measures, so that \(\mu_{0,\varepsilon}=\mu\), \(\mu_{1,\varepsilon}=\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon\), and, for every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
\mu_{t,\varepsilon}(x)
=\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R
\mu(x-t\sqrt\varepsilon z)e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z.
\]

\textbf{Step 1. Computing the flux.}
For \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\) and \(t\in[0,1]\),
\begin{align*}
\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} t}\int_\mathbb{R}\phi\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_{t,\varepsilon}
&=\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} t}\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R\int_\mathbb{R}
\phi(y+t\sqrt\varepsilon z)\mu(y)e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} y\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z\\
&=\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R\int_\mathbb{R}
\phi'(y+t\sqrt\varepsilon z)\sqrt\varepsilon z\,
\mu(y)e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} y \mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z
=\int_\mathbb{R}\phi'(x)\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}(x)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} x,
\end{align*}
where, by the change of variables \(y=x-t\sqrt\varepsilon z\),
\[
\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}(x)\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R
\sqrt\varepsilon z\,\mu(x-t\sqrt\varepsilon z)
e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z.
\]
Differentiation under the integral sign is justified since \(\phi'\) is bounded, \(\mu\in L^1\) and \(\int_{-R}^R |z|e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z<\infty\).
Thus \(\partial_t\mu_{t,\varepsilon}+\partial_x\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}=0\) in the sense of
distributions. Note that \(\mathfrak m_{0,\varepsilon}=0\) by
symmetry of the Gaussian kernel.

Let us estimate the total variation \(\|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\int_\mathbb{R}|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}|\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} x\). The flux depends linearly on \(\mu\): for \(f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})\), let
\[
\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}[f](x)\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R
\sqrt\varepsilon z\,f(x-t\sqrt\varepsilon z)
e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z,
\qquad\text{so that }\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}=\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}[\mu].
\]
We will use the following bounds on the moments of the truncated Gaussian, which are uniform in \(R\) and follow from an integration by parts and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality:
\begin{align}
\label{eq: 1D-second-moment}
\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R z^2e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z
&=1-\frac{2Re^{-R^2/2}}{c_R}\le1,
\\
\label{eq: 1D-first-moment}
\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R |z|e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z
&\le\left(\frac{1}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R z^2e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z\right)^{1/2}
\le1.
\end{align}
By Fubini's theorem, the translation invariance of the Lebesgue measure and \eqref{eq: 1D-first-moment}, we get
\[
\|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}[f]\|_{L^1}\le\sqrt\varepsilon\|f\|_{L^1}
\qquad\text{for every }f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}).
\]
If moreover \(f\in C_c^1(\mathbb{R})\), we write, with \(x_s\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} x-s\sqrt\varepsilon z\),
\[
f(x-t\sqrt\varepsilon z)
=f(x)-\int_0^t\sqrt\varepsilon z f'(x_s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s.
\]
Since the kernel is centered, that is,
\(\int_{-R}^R z e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z=0\),
the term containing \(f(x)\) cancels, so that, by \eqref{eq: 1D-second-moment},
\[
\|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}[f]\|_{L^1}
=\int_\mathbb{R}\left|\frac{\varepsilon}{c_R}\int_{-R}^R
z^2e^{-z^2/2}\int_0^tf'(x_s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z\right|\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} x
\le t\varepsilon\|f'\|_{L^1}
\le\varepsilon\|f'\|_{L^1}.
\]
Now let \((\mu^k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence in \(C_c^1(\mathbb{R})\)
such that \(\mu^k\to\mu\) in \(L^1\). Writing \(\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}=\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}[\mu-\mu^k]+\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}[\mu^k]\), we obtain, for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
\frac{\|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{\sqrt\varepsilon}
\le\|\mu-\mu^k\|_{L^1}
+\sqrt\varepsilon\|(\mu^k)'\|_{L^1}.
\]
Define, for \(r>0\),
\[
\omega(r)\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\left\{
\|\mu-\mu^k\|_{L^1}+r\|(\mu^k)'\|_{L^1}\right\}.
\]
For each fixed \(k\),
\(0\le\limsup_{r\downarrow0}\omega(r)\le\|\mu-\mu^k\|_{L^1}\), and
letting \(k\to\infty\) shows that \(\omega(r)\to0\) as \(r\to0\). Therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: 1D-flux-bound}
\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\frac{\|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{\sqrt\varepsilon}
\le\omega(\sqrt\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0
\qquad(\varepsilon\to0).
\end{equation}

\textbf{Step 2. Estimate of \(W_2(\mu,\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon)\).}
By Step~1, the curve \((\mu_{t,\varepsilon})_{t\in[0,1]}\) of probability measures with finite second moments solves, together with \((\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}})_{t\in[0,1]}\), the continuity equation, and it is weakly continuous, with \(\mu_{0,\varepsilon}=\mu\) and \(\mu_{1,\varepsilon}=\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon\). Since \(|z|\le R\) in the definition of \(\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}\), we have
\[
|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}(x)|
\le\frac{\sqrt\varepsilon R}{c_R}
\int_{-R}^R\mu(x-t\sqrt\varepsilon z)
e^{-z^2/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} z
=\sqrt\varepsilon R\,\mu_{t,\varepsilon}(x)
\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}\ll\mu_{t,\varepsilon}\), and the velocity field
\[
v_{t,\varepsilon}
\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} \operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}}{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_{t,\varepsilon}}
\quad\text{satisfies}\quad |v_{t,\varepsilon}|\le\sqrt\varepsilon R
\quad\mu_{t,\varepsilon}\text{-a.e.}
\]
By the Benamou--Brenier formula (see, e.g., \cite{santambrogioOptimalTransportApplied2015}), with \((\mu_{t,\varepsilon},v_{t,\varepsilon})_{t\in[0,1]}\) as a competitor, and by \eqref{eq: 1D-flux-bound}, we get
\begin{align*}
W_2^2(\mu,\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon)
&\le\int_0^1\int_\mathbb{R} |v_{t,\varepsilon}|^2
\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_{t,\varepsilon}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} t=\int_0^1\int_\mathbb{R} |v_{t,\varepsilon}|\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}|\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} t
\\
&\le\sqrt\varepsilon R\sup_{t\in[0,1]}
\|\operatorname{\mathfrak m_{t,\varepsilon}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le \varepsilon R\,\omega(\sqrt\varepsilon).
\end{align*}
Hence \(W_2(\mu,\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon)\le\sqrt R\,\sqrt{\omega(\sqrt\varepsilon)}\,\sqrt\varepsilon\), which concludes the proof, since \(\omega\) depends only on \(\mu\).

body_md: Since \(f\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz and \(\tau<1\), we have \((1-\tau)|x-y|\leq|\psi_\tau(x)-\psi_\tau(y)|\leq(1+\tau)|x-y|\) for \(x,y\in V\). Thus \(\psi_\tau\) is a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism onto its image, which is open by the invariance of domain theorem. By Rademacher's theorem, \(f\) is differentiable a.e.\ on \(V\), with \(\|Df\|\leq1\), and \(D\psi_\tau=\operatorname{Id}+\tau Df\) there. Since the determinant is Lipschitz on the set of matrices \(B\) with \(\|B\|\leq1\), there exists \(C_d\) such that \(|\det(\operatorname{Id}+B)-1|\leq C_d\|B\|\) for such \(B\). Applying this to \(B=\tau Df(x)\) gives \(|\mathcal J_{\psi_\tau}-1|\leq C_d\tau\) a.e.\ on \(V\). Finally, since the Lipschitz maps \(\psi_\tau\) and \(\kappa_\tau\) map negligible sets to negligible sets, for a.e.\ \(y\in\psi_\tau(V)\), \(\kappa_\tau\) is differentiable at \(y\) and \(\psi_\tau\) is differentiable at \(\kappa_\tau(y)\), so that \(\mathcal J_{\kappa_\tau}(y)=1/\mathcal J_{\psi_\tau}(\kappa_\tau(y))\) by the chain rule. Hence the same bound holds for \(\mathcal J_{\kappa_\tau}\), up to enlarging \(C_d\).

title: Proof
body_md:
We follow the proof of \hyperref[thm: A]{Theorem~A} given in \Cref{sec: selection}, and only indicate the changes. By compactness of \(\Sigma\cap\overline\omega\), the tubular coordinates, the normal ellipticity and the quadratic detachment hold on \(\Sigma\cap\omega\) with uniform constants (see \Cref{subsec: Convergence of the Gibbs measure and the geometric Laplace's method}), and \Cref{thm: euclidean-Gibbs} replaces \Cref{thm: convergence-Gibbs-measure}. In particular, the \(\Gamma\)-\(\liminf\) inequality (Step~1 of \Cref{subsec: selection-value-asymptotics}) is unchanged, and so is Step~3, since optimal plans are concentrated on \(\Sigma\cap\mathcal K\), where the density of \(\mathbb P_0\) with respect to \(\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\) is bounded from below.

It remains to adapt the \(\Gamma\)-\(\limsup\) inequality (Step~2 of \Cref{subsec: selection-value-asymptotics}). We fix \(\overline\gamma\in\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) with \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\), which is concentrated on \(\Sigma\cap\mathcal K\subset\Sigma\cap\omega\), and \(R\geq1\), and we define the normal perturbation \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\), its marginals \(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\) and its shadow \(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) as in \Cref{subsec: normal-recovery,subsec: correction}.

\textbf{Step 1. The marginals.} The marginal estimate of \Cref{thm: Wasserstein between the marginals} still holds: its proof only uses inverse charts of \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}^\Sigma_{M_i}\), which exist on \(\Sigma\cap\omega\) by \Cref{prop: twist-geometry} and finitely many of which cover the compact set \(\Sigma\cap\mathcal K\), and the integrability of the chart densities of \(\overline\gamma\). The energy estimate of \Cref{prop: shadow-energy} still holds as well: since \(\Omega\) is convex, the segments used in its proof stay in \(\operatorname{int}\Omega\), and \eqref{eq: gradient-distance} holds with \(\Sigma\) replaced by \(\Sigma\cap\overline\omega\). Indeed, a nearest point \(\bar y\) of \(y\in\operatorname{int}\Omega\) in the compact set \(\Sigma\cap\overline\omega\) lies in \(\operatorname{int}\Omega\), so that \(\nabla E(\bar y)=0\), and the segment \([\bar y,y]\) lies in \(\operatorname{int}\Omega\), whence \(|\nabla E(y)|\leq C_E\operatorname{dist}(y,\Sigma\cap\overline\omega)\) with \(C_E\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\sup_{\operatorname{int}\Omega}\|D^2E\|<\infty\) by \ref{H2'}. Hence, for fixed \(R\),
\[
W_2(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R},\mu_i)=o_R(\sqrt\varepsilon)\quad(i=1,2)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}-\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})=o_R(1).
\]

\textbf{Step 2. The entropy.} The entropy upper bound is the point to adapt since, as we wrote it, \(\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon)=+\infty\) in this case: \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) charges \(\Omega\setminus\mathcal K\), where \(\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\) vanishes. We therefore consider the entropy with respect to the modified marginals:
\[
 I_{\varepsilon,R}\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}
 \operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,
 \middle|\,\widetilde\mu_{1,\varepsilon,R}\otimes\widetilde\mu_{2,\varepsilon,R}\right).
\]
Since \(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}=Z_\varepsilon^{-1}e^{-E/\varepsilon}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)\), the shadow inequality (\Cref{prop: bound entropy shadow}) and Step~1 give, for fixed \(R\),
\[\begin{split}
 \operatorname{Ent}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\mathbb P_\varepsilon)&=\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)+\log Z_\varepsilon+\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\\
 &\leq I_{\varepsilon,R}+\log Z_\varepsilon+\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}-\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})+\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\\
 &\leq I_{\varepsilon,R}
 +\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}
 +\log Z_\varepsilon+o_R(1).
\end{split}
\]
It remains to show that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: euclidean-entropy-limsup}
 \limsup_{\varepsilon\to0}\left[
 I_{\varepsilon,R}
 +\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}
 +\log Z_\varepsilon\right]
 \leq\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)+b_R(\overline\gamma).
\end{equation}
Since \(|\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)-z|\leq\sqrt\varepsilon R\) for \(s\in\mathbb{B}_R\) and \(\overline\gamma\) is concentrated on \(\mathcal K\), for \(\sqrt\varepsilon R\leq1\) the measures \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) and \(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\) are concentrated on the fixed compact sets \(\mathcal K^1\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}:\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}},\mathcal K)\leq1\}\) and \(K_i^1\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,K_i)\leq1\}\). For an absolutely continuous probability measure \(\nu\) concentrated on a bounded set, we denote by \(\operatorname{Ent}(\nu)\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\operatorname{Ent}(\nu\,|\,\mathcal L)\) its entropy with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Since \(\widetilde\mu_{1,\varepsilon,R}\otimes\widetilde\mu_{2,\varepsilon,R}\) has the product of the marginal densities as density, we have
\[
I_{\varepsilon,R}=\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})-\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\mu_{1,\varepsilon,R})-\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\mu_{2,\varepsilon,R}),
\]
all these entropies being finite, since \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) has finite entropy and all the measures are concentrated on fixed bounded sets. Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: euclidean-entropy-decomposition}
I_{\varepsilon,R}
+\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}
+\log Z_\varepsilon
=\Bigl(\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})+\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}+\log Z_\varepsilon\Bigr)-\sum_{i=1}^2\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\right),
\end{equation}
and we pass to the limit in the two terms of the right-hand side in the next two steps.

\textbf{Step 3. The first term of \eqref{eq: euclidean-entropy-decomposition}.} Let \(\widetilde p_{\varepsilon,R}\) be the density \eqref{eq: normal-recovery-density} of \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\), and recall that \(K_R(z,s)=Z_R(z)^{-1}e^{-H_{z}E(s,s)/2}\) on \(\mathbb{B}_R\). Writing \(E(\Phi(z,\eta))=\frac12H_{z}E(\eta,\eta)+\mathcal R(z,\eta)\) with \(|\mathcal R(z,\eta)|\leq C|\eta|^3\), the quadratic terms cancel, and, for \(\mathcal H^d\)-a.e.\ \(z\in\Sigma\cap\mathcal K\) and \(s\in\mathbb{B}_R\),
\[
\log\Bigl(Z_\varepsilon e^{E/\varepsilon}\,\widetilde p_{\varepsilon,R}\Bigr)\bigl(\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)\bigr)
=\log\overline\rho(z)+\log\frac{Z_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^{k/2}Z_R(z)}+\frac{\mathcal R(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)}{\varepsilon}-\log\mathcal J_\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s).
\]
We integrate this identity against \(K_R(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma(z)\), which gives the first term of \eqref{eq: euclidean-entropy-decomposition} by \eqref{eq: recovery sequence with wrong marginals 1}. The integral of the last two terms is bounded by \(C\sqrt\varepsilon(M_1+M_3)\to0\), by \eqref{eq: tube-jacobian-rescaled} and \eqref{eq: gaussian-moments}. Moreover, since \(Z_\varepsilon=(2\pi\varepsilon)^{k/2}(Z_0+o(1))\) by \Cref{thm: euclidean-Gibbs}, we have, uniformly in \(z\), with \(Z_\infty\) as in \Cref{lemma: convergence entropy},
\[
\log\frac{Z_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^{k/2}Z_R(z)}=\log\Bigl(Z_0\sqrt{\detH_{z}E}\Bigr)+\log\frac{Z_\infty(z)}{Z_R(z)}+o(1).
\]
Since \(\int_\Sigma|\log\overline\rho|\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma<\infty\) (because \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\)) and \(\mathbb P_0\) has density \(Z_0^{-1}(\detH_{z}E)^{-1/2}\rho(z)\) with respect to \(\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\) on \(\Sigma\cap\mathcal K\), we obtain
\begin{align*}
\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\Bigl(\operatorname{Ent}(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R})+\frac1\varepsilon\int E\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}+\log Z_\varepsilon\Bigr)
&=\int_\Sigma\log\frac{Z_0\,\overline\rho\sqrt{\detH_{z}E}}{\rho}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma+\int_\Sigma\log\rho\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma+b_R(\overline\gamma)\\
&=\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)+\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_1)+\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_2)+b_R(\overline\gamma),
\end{align*}
where we used that \(\overline\gamma\) has marginals \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) and \(\rho=\rho_1\otimes\rho_2\), so that \(\int\log\rho\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma=\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_1)+\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_2)\).

\textbf{Step 4. The marginal entropies in \eqref{eq: euclidean-entropy-decomposition}.} By \eqref{eq: normal-perturbation-W2}, \(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\rightharpoonup\mu_i\) as \(\varepsilon\to0\), and all these measures are concentrated on the compact set \(K_i^1\). Since \(\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot)=\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot\,|\,\mathcal L_{|K_i^1})\) on such measures, and the relative entropy with respect to a finite measure is weakly lower semicontinuous, we get
\[
\liminf_{\varepsilon\to0}\operatorname{Ent}\left(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\right)\geq\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_i),\qquad i=1,2.
\]

\textbf{Conclusion.} Plugging Steps~3 and~4 into \eqref{eq: euclidean-entropy-decomposition} gives \eqref{eq: euclidean-entropy-limsup}, hence
\[
\limsup_{\varepsilon\to0}\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\,|\,\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon})\leq\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)+b_R(\overline\gamma).
\] The diagonal argument of Step~2 of \Cref{subsec: selection-value-asymptotics} then provides a recovery sequence, and the remaining conclusions follow as in the proof of \hyperref[thm: A]{Theorem~A}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Brenier's theorem, in the quadratic case the optimal plan \(\overline\gamma\) is unique and given by \(\overline\gamma=(\operatorname{id},T)_{\#}\mu_1\), where \(T\) is the Brenier map between \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\). Consequently, \(\overline\gamma\) is supported on the graph \(\{(x_1,T(x_1)) \,|\, x_1\in\operatorname{spt}\mu_1\}\subseteq\Sigma\) and the tangent space of \(\Sigma\) is
\[
T_{(x_1,T(x_1))}\Sigma=\operatorname{Img}\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Id}\\ DT(x_1)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence, the Hessian of the duality gap is given by
    \begin{align*}     
    \operatorname{Hess} E\big(x_1,T(x_1)\big) 
    &=\begin{pmatrix}
        \operatorname{Id}- D^2\overline\varphi_1(x_1) & -\operatorname{Id}
        \\ 
        -\operatorname{Id}  & \operatorname{Id}- D^2\overline\varphi_2(T(x_1))
    \end{pmatrix}
    \\
    &=\begin{pmatrix}
        DT(x_1) & -\operatorname{Id}
        \\ 
        -\operatorname{Id}  & DT(x_1)^{-1}
    \end{pmatrix},
\end{align*}
where we used that \(T=\operatorname{Id}-\nabla\overline\varphi_1\) (from \(\nabla_{x_1}E=0\) on \(\Sigma\)) and that \(\operatorname{Id}-D^2\overline\varphi_2(T(x_1))=DT(x_1)^{-1}\), obtained by differentiating the identity \(x_1=T(x_1)-\nabla\overline\varphi_2(T(x_1))\) (from \(\nabla_{x_2}E=0\) on \(\Sigma\)).
We define \(n(x_1)\), the matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of the normal space \(N_{(x_1,T(x_1))}\Sigma\), as 
\[n(x_1) \stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} \begin{pmatrix}
    -DT(x_1) \\
        \operatorname{Id}
        \end{pmatrix}(\operatorname{Id}+ DT(x_1)^2)^{-1/2}.\]
The reduced Hessian of \(E\) in the normal directions is therefore
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Hess}^\perp &E\big(x_1,T(x_1)\big)
\\
&= n(x_1)^\top \operatorname{Hess} E\big(x_1,T(x_1)\big)n(x_1)
\\
&= (DT(x_1)^2 + \operatorname{Id})^{-1/2}\Big( DT(x_1)^3 + 2DT(x_1) + DT(x_1)^{-1}\Big) (DT(x_1)^2 + \operatorname{Id})^{-1/2}
\\
&=DT(x_1) + DT(x_1)^{-1}
\end{align*}
For \(\mu_1\)-almost every \(x_1\), with \(x_2=T(x_1)\)  the Monge-Ampère equation gives
\[
\det DT(x_1)=\frac{\rho_1(x_1)}{\rho_2(T(x_1))}=\frac{\rho_1(x_1)}{\rho_2(x_2)}
\]
and therefore
\[
\det\big(\operatorname{Hess}^\perp E(x_1,x_2)\big)^{-1/2}
=\left(\frac{\rho_1(x_1)}{\rho_2(x_2)}\right)^{1/2}\det\big(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\big)^{-1/2}.
\]
Consequently, writing \(\overline\rho\) for the density of \(\overline\gamma\) with respect to \(\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\), we obtain
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)
&=\int_{\Sigma}
\log\left(
\frac{\overline\rho(x_1,x_2)}{Z_0^{-1}\det\big(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\big)^{-1/2}\,
\rho_1(x_1)^{3/2}\rho_2(x_2)^{1/2}}
\right)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma(x_1,x_2)
\\
&=\operatorname{Ent}\left(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\right)
-\frac32\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_1)-\frac12\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_2)
\\
&\qquad 
+\frac12\int\log\det\big(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\big)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_1(x_1)
+\log Z_0 .
\end{align*}
We now compute \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma})\) using the graph structure of \(\Sigma\). Since \(\Sigma\) is parametrized by \(x_1\mapsto(x_1,T(x_1))\), whose differential \(\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Id}\\ DT(x_1)\end{pmatrix}\) has Gram matrix \(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\), the area formula gives
\[
\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}=\det\big(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\big)^{1/2}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} x_1 .
\]
Hence
\[
\overline\rho(x_1,T(x_1))=\rho_1(x_1)\det\big(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\big)^{-1/2}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Ent}\left(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\right)
&=\int\log\overline\rho\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma
=\int\log\Big(\rho_1(x_1)\det\big(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\big)^{-1/2}\Big)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_1(x_1)
\\
&=\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_1)-\frac12\int\log\det\big(\operatorname{Id}+DT(x_1)^2\big)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_1(x_1).
\end{align*}
Plugging this into the previous identity, the \(\log\det\) terms cancel and we get
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)-\log Z_0
&=\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_1)-\frac32\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_1)-\frac12\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_2)
\\
&=-\frac12\big(\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_1)+\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_2)\big).
\end{align*}
Finally, we conclude by \Cref{thm: euclidean-selection}.

\[
\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}2\pi\rho_1(x_1)\rho_2(T_j(x_1))=\rho_1(x_1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}2\pi\rho_1(T_j^{-1}(x_2))\rho_2(x_2)=\rho_2(x_2),
\]
so that \(\gamma_0\in\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\). Moreover, \(\gamma_0\) and \(\mathbb P_0\) are equivalent, with
\[
\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma_0}{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathbb P_0}(x_1,x_2)=g(u_1)\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\frac{1-e^{-2}}2\,e^{2u_1},
\]
which only depends on \(x_1\). Hence, for every \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) such that \(\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\),
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)
&=\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\gamma_0)+\int\log g(u_1)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma(x_1,x_2)
=\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\gamma_0)+\int\log g(u_1)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_1(x_1)\\
&=\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\gamma_0)+\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma_0\,|\,\mathbb P_0).

title: Proof
body_md:
The proofs of \Cref{sec: gibbs,sec: selection} and of \Cref{subsec: Convergence of the Gibbs measure and the geometric Laplace's method} use the two-marginal structure at three places only.

\textbf{(i) Normal ellipticity.} In \Cref{prop: twist-geometry}, \eqref{eq: normal-ellipticity} is deduced from the non-degeneracy of \(c\). Here, it follows from \eqref{eq: multimarginal-rank}, the positive semidefiniteness of \(\operatorname{Hess} E\) on \(\Sigma\), and the compactness of \(\Sigma\).

\textbf{(ii) Local normal frames.} A \(C^{1,1}\) submanifold admits local Lipschitz orthonormal frames of its normal bundle; see the Gram--Schmidt construction in \cite[Section~2.3.1, arXiv version]{minguzzi2015convex}. We choose a finite cover \((U_a)_a\) of \(\Sigma\) by relatively compact patches with such frames \(n_a\), and a subordinate Lipschitz partition of unity \((\chi_a)_a\). For \(r>0\) sufficiently small, the maps
\[
\Phi_a(z,s)\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} z+n_a(z)s,
\qquad z\in U_a,\quad s\in\mathbb{B}_r,
\]
are bi-Lipschitz tubular parametrizations, by the positive-reach property used in \Cref{subsec:structure}. Since the frames are Lipschitz, the proof of \Cref{lemma: determinant of Phi} applies on each patch, and \eqref{eq: tube-jacobian-expansion} holds almost everywhere, with uniform bounds over the finite cover. The area formula then gives
\[
\int_{\Sigma_r}h\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}_\Omega
=\sum_a\int_{U_a}\chi_a(z)\int_{\mathbb{B}_r}
h\bigl(\Phi_a(z,s)\bigr)\mathcal J_{\Phi_a}(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^d(z)
\]
for every nonnegative Borel function \(h\). We apply the three-region Laplace argument to each integral in this sum. The weights \(\chi_a\) depend only on \(z\), and the resulting limits sum to the desired integral because \(\sum_a\chi_a=1\).

On overlaps, \(n_b(z)=n_a(z)O_{ab}(z)\) with \(O_{ab}(z)\in O(k)\). The coordinate change \((z,s)\mapsto(z,O_{ab}(z)s)\) has absolute Jacobian one almost everywhere, even though \(O_{ab}\) depends on \(z\). It also preserves the normal Gaussian measure and \(\mathbb{B}_R\), that is 
\[
H_b=O_{ab}^{\top}H_aO_{ab},
\qquad
K_b(z,s)=K_a(z,O_{ab}s),
\] where \(H_a(z)\) is the matrix of the normal Hessian in the local orthonormal frame \(n_a(z)\). Thus the local normal perturbations agree on overlaps and define the recovery measure in \Cref{subsec: normal-recovery}. In the Euclidean case, we use a finite cover of the compact portion \(\Sigma\cap\overline\omega\) appearing in the Laplace proof.

With (i) and (ii), the proofs of \Cref{thm: convergence-Gibbs-measure} (\Cref{subsec: Convergence of the Gibbs measure and the geometric Laplace's method}), of \Cref{lemma: convergence entropy}, \Cref{prop: control of the shadow entropy}, \Cref{prop: shadow-energy}, and of Steps~1 and~3 of \Cref{subsec: selection-value-asymptotics} apply verbatim, with sums over \(i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\); recall that Step~3 only uses that \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_{M_1}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz.

\textbf{(iii) Marginal estimate.} The proof of \Cref{thm: Wasserstein between the marginals} uses local inverses of \(\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_{M_i}^\Sigma\), which, for \(N\geq3\), may have critical points (vertical branches). Let \(\overline\gamma\) be the plan fixed in Step~2 of \Cref{subsec: selection-value-asymptotics}. We fix \(i\) and \(R\geq1\), and write \(p\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\operatorname{\mathrm{proj}}_{M_i}^\Sigma\), \(\mu\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\mu_i\) and \(\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}\). Let \(C\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\{z\in\Sigma:\operatorname{rank} Dp(z)<d\}\). By Sard's theorem, \(p(C)\) is Lebesgue-negligible, so that \(\overline\gamma(C)\leq\mu(p(C))=0\). Given \(\eta>0\), we choose an open set \(V\supset p(C)\) such that \(\mu(V)<\eta\), and we split \(\overline\gamma=\overline\gamma^b+\overline\gamma^g\), with \(\overline\gamma^b\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\overline\gamma\mathbin{\vrule height 1.6ex depth 0pt width
0.13ex\vrule height 0.13ex depth 0pt width 1.3ex} p^{-1}(V)\). Accordingly, \(\mu=\mu^b+\mu^g\) and \(\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon=\widetilde\mu^b_\varepsilon+\widetilde\mu^g_\varepsilon\), where \(\mu^b\), \(\mu^g\) and \(\widetilde\mu^b_\varepsilon\), \(\widetilde\mu^g_\varepsilon\) are the \(i\)-th marginals of \(\overline\gamma^b\), \(\overline\gamma^g\) and of their normal perturbations, defined by \eqref{eq: recovery sequence with wrong marginals 1}. On the compact set \(\Sigma\setminus p^{-1}(V)\), \(p\) is a local diffeomorphism, and the proof of \Cref{thm: Wasserstein between the marginals}, which only uses that the chart densities are integrable, gives \(W_2^2(\mu^g,\widetilde\mu^g_\varepsilon)=o_\eta(\varepsilon)\), where \(W_2\) is extended to measures of equal mass. On the other hand, since \(|p(\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s))-p(z)|\leq\sqrt\varepsilon|s|\), the map \((z,s)\mapsto(p(z),p(\Phi(z,\sqrt\varepsilon s)))\) pushes \(K_R(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma^b(z)\) forward to a coupling of \(\mu^b\) and \(\widetilde\mu^b_\varepsilon\) with quadratic cost at most
\[
\varepsilon\int_\Sigma\int_{\mathbb{B}_R}|s|^2K_R(z,s)\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma^b(z)\leq M_2\,\varepsilon\,\overline\gamma^b(\Sigma)=M_2\,\varepsilon\,\mu(V)\leq M_2\,\varepsilon\,\eta,
\]
by \eqref{eq: gaussian-moments}. Gluing the two couplings, we get \(W_2^2(\mu,\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon)\leq o_\eta(\varepsilon)+M_2\varepsilon\eta\). Letting \(\varepsilon\to0\), then \(\eta\to0\), gives \(W_2(\mu,\widetilde\mu_\varepsilon)=o_R(\sqrt\varepsilon)\), which completes the proof.

\begin{align*}
\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}|x_i-x_j|^2
&=
\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}
\left(
|x_i|^2+|x_j|^2-2\langle x_i, x_j\rangle
\right)
\\
&=
(N-1)\sum_{i=1}^N|x_i|^2
-2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\langle x_i, x_j\rangle.
\end{align*}
On the other hand, \(|\sum_{i=1}^N x_i|^2
= \sum_{i=1}^N|x_i|^2 + 2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\langle x_i, x_j\rangle\). Therefore, \(\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}|x_i-x_j|^2
=
N\sum_{i=1}^N|x_i|^2-|
\sum_{i=1}^N x_i|^2\). Since \(x_i\in \mathbb S^1\), one has \(|x_i|=1\), and hence \(
\sum_{i=1}^N|x_i|^2=N\). Consequently, \(c(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})=|
\sum_{i=1}^N x_i|^2-N^2\).
Thus, for every \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu_i)\),
\[
\int_{(\mathbb S^1)^N}c(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})\,\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
=
\int_{(\mathbb S^1)^N}
\Big|
\sum_{i=1}^N x_i
\Big|^2
\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})
-
N^2.
\]
Since \(N^2\) is independent of \(\gamma\), minimizing the original
cost is equivalent to minimizing
\[

\Big|
\sum_{i=1}^N x_i
\Big|^2
\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}).
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
We verify the normal-rank hypothesis and apply the Gibbs formula
of \Cref{thm: multimarginal-extension}:
    \[\mathbb P_0 = \frac{1}{Z_0} (\det \operatorname{Hess}^\perp E)^{-1/2} \prod_{i=1}^N \rho_i \mathcal H^1_{| \Sigma}.\]
We compute the normal Hessian and the normalization. For \(i=1,2,3\), introduce the geodesics
\[\nu_i(\tau ) =\exp_{x_i}(\tau v_i), \]
where \(v_i \in T_{x_i}\mathbb S^1\). We also introduce \(S(\tau) \stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} \nu_1(\tau) + \nu_2(\tau) + \nu_3(\tau)\), then we have
\[\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} }{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} \tau }E\big( \nu_1(\tau) , \nu_2(\tau) , \nu_3(\tau)\big) = 2 \langle \dot S(\tau) , S(\tau) \rangle, \]
and 
\[\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}^2 }{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\tau^2}E\big( \nu_1(\tau) , \nu_2(\tau) , \nu_3(\tau)\big) = 2\langle \ddot S(\tau) , S(\tau)\rangle + 2|\dot S(\tau)|^2.\]
Thus, for \(\tau =0\), since \( S(0)= 0\), we obtain
\[\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}^2 }{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\tau^2}E\big( \nu_1(\tau) , \nu_2(\tau) , \nu_3(\tau)\big)\Big|_{\tau=0}= 2|v_1 + v_2 + v_3|^2,\]
and denoting \(V = (v_1, v_2,v_3)\) we have 
\[\operatorname{Hess} E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})[V,V]=2|v_1 + v_2 + v_3|^2. \]
Let \(e_i \stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} Jx_i\), where
\[
J=
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & -1\\
1 & 0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
so that \(e_i\) is a unit tangent vector to \(\mathbb S^1\) at \(x_i\). Then
\[
E_1=(e_1,0,0),\qquad E_2=(0,e_2,0),\qquad E_3=(0,0,e_3)
\]
is an orthonormal basis of \(T_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}(\mathbb S^1)^3\). We obtain
\[
\operatorname{Hess} E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})[E_i,E_i]=2,
\qquad
\operatorname{Hess} E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})[E_i,E_j]
=
2\langle e_i,e_j\rangle
=
2\langle x_i,x_j\rangle
=
-1,
\]
for \(i\neq j\), since \(\operatorname{\textbf{x}}\in\Sigma\). Hence
\[
[\operatorname{Hess} E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})]
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & -1 & -1\\
-1 & 2 & -1\\
-1 & -1 & 2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
T_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}\Sigma
=
\operatorname{span} \{E_1+E_2+E_3\},
\]
and therefore
\[
N_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}\Sigma
=
\left\{
aE_1+bE_2+cE_3
\;|\;
a+b+c=0
\right\}.
\]
On this normal space, the above matrix acts as \(3\operatorname{Id}\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{Hess}^\perp E(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})=3\operatorname{Id}_{N_{\operatorname{\textbf{x}}}\Sigma},
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{Hess} E=2=(N-1)d\), as required
by \Cref{thm: multimarginal-extension}, and
\(\det\operatorname{Hess}^\perp E=9\). The induced arclength must also
be included in the normalization: the maps \(F_\pm\) have speed
\(\sqrt3\) when the unit circle is parametrized by arclength. Hence
\[
 \mathcal H^1(\Sigma_\pm)=2\pi\sqrt3,
 \qquad Z_0=(2\pi)^{-3}\frac{4\pi\sqrt3}{3}
 =\frac{1}{2\sqrt3\,\pi^2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \mathbb P_0=\frac{1}{4\pi\sqrt3}\mathcal H^1_{|\Sigma}
 =\frac12(\gamma_++\gamma_-).
\]
Since \(\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot \,|\,\mathbb P_0) \) is nonnegative and \(\mathbb P_0 \in \Pi(\mu_i)\), we conclude that the selected transport plan is \(\mathbb P_0\).

body_md:
\label{thm: harmonic-Rd}
Assume (M). Then the conclusions of \Cref{thm: convergence-Gibbs-measure} and of \hyperref[thm: A]{Theorem~A} hold, with \(\Pi(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_N)\) in place of \(\Pi(\mu_1,\mu_2)\), \(k=d\), and
\[
\mathbb P_0\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\frac{\rho\,\mathcal H^{(N-1)d}_{|\Sigma_b}}{\int_{\Sigma_b}\rho\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^{(N-1)d}},
\qquad
Z_0\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}(2N)^{-d/2}\int_{\Sigma_b}\rho\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^{(N-1)d}.
\]
Moreover, the selected plan is \(\gamma_M\), and
\[
\min\mathcal F_\varepsilon=\mathsf{OT}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_N)+\frac d2\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\Bigl(\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_{i_0})+\frac d2\log\pi\Bigr)+o(\varepsilon),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_{i_0})\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\int\rho_{i_0}\log\rho_{i_0}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} x\).

title: Proof
body_md:
We follow the proofs of \Cref{thm: euclidean-Gibbs,thm: euclidean-selection}, with \(\Sigma_b\) in place of the \(d\)-dimensional contact set: these proofs do not use the dimension of the contact set, and they are simpler here, since the normal coordinates are global and \(E\) is exactly quadratic in them.

\textbf{Step 1. Gibbs measures and \(\Gamma\)-\(\liminf\).} The proof of \Cref{thm: euclidean-Gibbs} applies with \(\mathcal H^{(N-1)d}\) in place of \(\mathcal H^d\), \(\mathcal R\equiv0\), \(\mathcal J_\Phi\equiv1\) and \(\mathcal T_r=\Sigma_r\). Its assumption \(\mathcal H^{(N-1)d}(\Sigma_b\cap\partial\mathcal K)=0\), where \(\mathcal K=\prod_iK_i\), follows from \(\mathcal L^d(\partial K_i)=0\): for \(j\neq i\), parametrizing \(\Sigma_b\) by the coordinates \((x_l)_{l\neq j}\), the set \(\Sigma_b\cap\{x_i\in\partial K_i\}\) is the image of a negligible set by a Lipschitz map. Moreover, \(Z_0>0\), since \(\rho>0\) \(\gamma_M\)-a.e.\ and \(\gamma_M\ll\mathcal H^{(N-1)d}_{|\Sigma_b}\) (see Step~2). Since \(\detH_{z}E=(2N)^d\) is constant, this gives \(\operatorname{\mathbb{P}_\varepsilon}\rightharpoonup\mathbb P_0\) and \(Z_\varepsilon=(2\pi\varepsilon)^{d/2}(Z_0+o(1))\), and the \(\Gamma\)-\(\liminf\) inequality follows as in Step~1 of \Cref{subsec: selection-value-asymptotics}.

\textbf{Step 2. A finite-entropy optimal plan.} Parametrizing \(\Sigma_b\) by \((x_i)_{i\neq i_0}\), whose surface Jacobian is \(N^{d/2}\), we get \(\gamma_M=N^{-d/2}\prod_{i\neq i_0}\rho_i(x_i)\,\mathcal H^{(N-1)d}_{|\Sigma_b}\). Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq: harmonic-Rd-density}
\frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma_M}{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathbb P_0}(\operatorname{\textbf{x}})=\frac{C_M}{\rho_{i_0}(x_{i_0})},
\qquad
C_M\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=} N^{-d/2}\int_{\Sigma_b}\rho\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^{(N-1)d},
\end{equation}
and \(\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma_M\,|\,\mathbb P_0)=\log C_M-\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_{i_0})<\infty\), since \(\rho_{i_0}\) is bounded with compact support. This replaces Step~3 of \Cref{subsec: selection-value-asymptotics}, where the bound \(\overline\gamma\leq\beta\mathcal H^d_{|\Sigma}\) used \(\dim\Sigma=d\).

\textbf{Step 3. The marginals.} Fix \(\overline\gamma\in\Pi(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_N)\) with \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\), and \(R\geq1\). Since \(H_{z}E=2N\,I_d\) does not depend on \(z\), neither does the kernel \(K_R(z,s)=K_R(s)\propto e^{-N|s|^2}\mathbf 1_{\mathbb{B}_R}(s)\). Hence, by \eqref{eq: recovery sequence with wrong marginals 1}, \(\widetilde\gamma_{\varepsilon,R}\) is the law of \(Z+\sqrt{\varepsilon/N}\,(S,\ldots,S)\), where \(Z\sim\overline\gamma\) and \(S\sim K_R\) are independent, and its \(i\)-th marginal is
\[
\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R}=\mu_i*\eta_\varepsilon,
\qquad
\eta_\varepsilon\stackrel{\text{def.}}{=}\text{law of }\sqrt{\varepsilon/N}\,S.
\]
Writing \(\sqrt{\varepsilon/N}\,S=\sqrt{\varepsilon/(2N^2)}\,S'\), where \(S'=\sqrt{2N}\,S\) has density proportional to \(e^{-|s'|^2/2}\) on \(\mathbb{B}_{\sqrt{2N}R}\), we are in the setting of \Cref{prop: 1D}, with \(\varepsilon/(2N^2)\) and \(\sqrt{2N}R\) in place of \(\varepsilon\) and \(R\). Its proof applies verbatim in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and gives \(W_2(\widetilde\mu_{i,\varepsilon,R},\mu_i)=o_R(\sqrt\varepsilon)\).

\textbf{Step 4. Energy and entropy.} The rest of the proof of \Cref{thm: euclidean-selection} is unchanged. The energy estimate of \Cref{prop: shadow-energy} holds, since \(|\nabla E(\mathbf y)|=2N\operatorname{dist}(\mathbf y,\Sigma_b)\) for every \(\mathbf y\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^N\). In Step~3 of the proof of \Cref{thm: euclidean-selection}, the remainder and Jacobian terms vanish, and \(\int|\log\overline\rho|\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma<\infty\) follows from \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\) and \(\int|\log\rho|\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\overline\gamma\leq\sum_i\int\rho_i|\log\rho_i|\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} x<\infty\).

\textbf{Step 5. Selection and value.} By \eqref{eq: harmonic-Rd-density}, \(\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\gamma_M/\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mathbb P_0\) only depends on \(x_{i_0}\). Hence, for every \(\gamma\in\Pi(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_N)\) with \(\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)<\infty\), as in the proof of \Cref{prop: MPW-selection},
\[
\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\mathbb P_0)=\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\gamma_M)+\int\log\frac{C_M}{\rho_{i_0}}\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d}\mu_{i_0}=\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma\,|\,\gamma_M)+\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma_M\,|\,\mathbb P_0),
\]
so that \(\gamma_M\) is the unique minimizer of \(\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot\,|\,\mathbb P_0)\) on \(\Pi(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_N)\), that is, the selected plan. Finally, since \(C_M=2^{d/2}Z_0\),
\[
\min\mathcal F^{(1)}=\operatorname{Ent}(\gamma_M\,|\,\mathbb P_0)-\log Z_0-\frac d2\log(2\pi)
=-\operatorname{Ent}(\mu_{i_0})-\frac d2\log\pi,
\]
and the expansion of \(\min\mathcal F_\varepsilon\) follows from \hyperref[thm: A]{Theorem~A}.
